title: Prompting Isn’t the Skill
kicker: Keynote / AI & the future of work
subtitle: Bring your humanity to AI.
premise: Your curiosity, lived experience, empathy, and judgment shape what you ask of AI—and what you do with its answers. This talk puts those human strengths to work through a practical approach you can use the next time you open a conversation.

ideas.statement: Your curiosity gives AI direction.
ideas.title: Start with what you know.
ideas.copy: Use your curiosity and experience to get clear on the problem. Explain what you want to accomplish, who the work is for, and what matters in their situation.
ideas.question: “What does someone actually need from this?”

ideas.statement: A fluent answer still needs your judgment.
ideas.title: Know what good looks like.
ideas.copy: Check the facts, challenge assumptions, and consider whose perspective is missing. Bring your knowledge of the people and situation to deciding whether the answer is accurate, appropriate, and useful.
ideas.question: “Is this accurate—and does it make sense for these people?”

ideas.statement: Your care shapes the final result.
ideas.title: Make the next version more useful.
ideas.copy: Give specific feedback, add missing context, and check the revision against the need you started with. Consider how it will land with the people using it, and take responsibility for what you share.
ideas.question: “What needs to change for this to be useful?”

takeaway: A practical way to approach AI: define the work, question the answer, and improve the result—with your curiosity, empathy, and judgment guiding each step.

title: You Hired AI. Now Manage It.
subtitle: 10 ways to put AI to work—and manage it well.
premise: AI can help you research, draft, organize, analyze, and rehearse. The opportunity is knowing which job to give it—and how to manage that job well. This talk explores ten useful roles for AI, with concrete assignments, management habits, and ways to check the work.
navigationLabel: Explore ten roles you can give AI

ideas.statement: Turn sources into a useful brief.
ideas.title: Research assistant
ideas.copy: Compare supplied sources, summarize findings around a question, and identify gaps worth investigating. Delegate the first pass at making sense of the material.
ideas.question: Define the question and source set. Ask for references for key claims, then check those references before relying on the brief.

ideas.statement: Find the patterns worth a closer look.
ideas.title: Data analyst
ideas.copy: Explore a supplied dataset, compare categories, and surface trends or exceptions. Use it to prepare tables, explain calculations, and suggest questions for further analysis.
ideas.question: Define the measures. Ask for calculations you can inspect, and check key results against the source data.

ideas.statement: Get several directions on the table.
ideas.title: Brainstorming partner
ideas.copy: Generate different approaches to a challenge, from a new offer to a team activity. Explore combinations and alternatives before investing in one direction.
ideas.question: Give it constraints and ask for distinct options. Generate possibilities first; then evaluate them against your criteria.

ideas.statement: Give your proposal a tough first review.
ideas.title: Critical reviewer
ideas.copy: Review a draft for unsupported assumptions, inconsistencies, missing steps, and likely objections. Use the critique to prepare the work for a real audience.
ideas.question: Assign a review rubric and ask for specific examples. Evaluate the criticism before deciding what to change.

ideas.statement: Turn your notes into a first draft.
ideas.title: Draft writer
ideas.copy: Turn your facts, notes, and objective into a draft email, brief, outline, or proposal. Give it the material and let it assemble a version you can work with.
ideas.question: Provide the source facts and desired structure. Have it mark unknowns so you can supply what is missing.

ideas.statement: Make the writing easier to use.
ideas.title: Editor
ideas.copy: Tighten a draft, improve its structure, adjust the tone, or adapt it for a particular audience. Use it to develop clearer versions of what you already mean.
ideas.question: Set the scope of the edit and provide a voice example. Ask it to explain substantive changes so you can preserve the meaning.

ideas.statement: Give the goal a workable sequence.
ideas.title: Project planner
ideas.copy: Break a goal into tasks, dependencies, milestones, and a draft timeline. Use the plan to surface the decisions and resources the work will need.
ideas.question: Supply deadlines, resources, and constraints. Have it label assumptions, then confirm capacity before committing to the plan.

ideas.statement: Turn the discussion into a clear record.
ideas.title: Meeting assistant
ideas.copy: Turn supplied notes or a transcript into a decision log, action list, and unresolved questions. Make it easier for people to see what was agreed and what still needs attention.
ideas.question: Separate decisions from suggestions. Include owners and dates only where agreed, then confirm the record with participants.

ideas.statement: Rehearse before the real conversation.
ideas.title: Practice partner
ideas.copy: Simulate an interview, customer conversation, or presentation Q&A. Try different responses and practice handling follow-up questions before the real event.
ideas.question: Describe the scenario, role, and difficulty. Ask for one question at a time, then request feedback against clear criteria.

ideas.statement: Turn existing know-how into instructions.
ideas.title: Process documenter
ideas.copy: Organize existing instructions and expert notes into a checklist, FAQ, or draft procedure. Give repeatable work a structure that someone else can follow.
ideas.question: Have it flag missing steps. Test the draft with someone who knows the task and revise it before sharing.

takeaway: Ten roles you can put AI to work in, plus a practical way to manage each one: what to delegate, how to direct it, and what to check before you use the result.

title: From Copilot to Coworker
subtitle: When AI takes on work, what do people get back?
signature: Better work. More room for people.
premise: When AI takes on a task, leaders still have choices to make about how the team works. Using a recurring reporting process as an example, this talk explores what to stop, which decisions people should own, and how to use any capacity created for work that needs their attention.

ideas.statement: A faster report can leave the same bottleneck.
ideas.title: Redesign the whole routine.
ideas.copy: Imagine AI prepares a first draft of your weekly report. Follow what happens next: the checks, approvals, meetings, and follow-up. Decide which steps still help someone act and which have become repetition.
ideas.question: “What could we stop doing if this part of the work changed?”

ideas.statement: People need clarity about what they still own.
ideas.title: Make responsibility explicit.
ideas.copy: Give the team clear expectations for checking the report, investigating exceptions, and deciding what to do. Include the context, authority, and support they need to exercise judgment.
ideas.question: “Which decisions need a person who knows the situation?”

ideas.statement: Time saved deserves a deliberate purpose.
ideas.title: Choose what the team gets back.
ideas.copy: Agree how any capacity created will be used: more time with customers, deeper analysis, coaching, or a more manageable workload. Test the new routine with the team and check whether the work has improved overall.
ideas.question: “What becomes possible for people when this takes less effort?”

takeaway: A practical way to rethink one recurring workflow: remove outdated steps, make human decisions explicit, and choose how to use any capacity created.

title: Stop Calling It a People Problem
subtitle: Give people what they need to do good work.
premise: When work falls short, leaders need to understand what is getting in the way. Expectations, tools, skills, priorities, and feedback all shape what people can do. This talk helps leaders investigate the gap, have a useful conversation, and take responsibility for the support their teams need.

ideas.statement: Useful feedback starts with a clear expectation.
ideas.title: Get specific about what happened.
ideas.copy: Describe the work you expected and what you observed. Ask how the person understood the task and what feedback they had along the way. Establish a shared picture of what good work looks like.
ideas.question: “What did we expect, what happened, and what do we still need to understand?”

ideas.statement: Conditions shape what people can do.
ideas.title: Look at the work around the person.
ideas.copy: Ask about priorities, tools, time, authority, and the pressures people are managing. Look for conflicting instructions or incentives. Listen for what makes the expected behavior difficult in practice.
ideas.question: “What is making the right thing difficult to do?”

ideas.statement: Support should fit the obstacle.
ideas.title: Match the response to the cause.
ideas.copy: Choose practice for a skill gap, clearer priorities for competing demands, or better tools for repeated friction. Agree on what the employee will do and what you will change as their leader, then set a time to check progress.
ideas.question: “What does this person need from me to succeed?”

takeaway: A practical way to address performance: describe the gap, understand the conditions, and agree on what the employee and leader will each do next.

title: The Best Process Is the One People Actually Use
subtitle: Design for the way people actually work.
premise: A process should help people do their work well. Shortcuts, repeated questions, and unofficial spreadsheets reveal where the design makes that harder. This talk shows leaders how to learn from the people doing the work, remove unnecessary effort, and build a process that holds up in everyday use.

ideas.statement: Workarounds tell you something.
ideas.title: Watch what people actually do.
ideas.copy: Follow a real task with someone who does it regularly. Notice the spreadsheets, messages, and extra steps that keep it moving. Ask what each workaround solves before deciding what to change.
ideas.question: “What makes the unofficial way easier?”

ideas.statement: Make the useful path easier.
ideas.title: Remove effort that adds no value.
ideas.copy: Look for duplicate entry, unclear decisions, and information people have to hunt down. Simplify those points while keeping necessary checks. Make the next action and the person responsible easy to identify.
ideas.question: “Which part asks people to work around the design?”

ideas.statement: A process proves itself in use.
ideas.title: Learn from the next real attempt.
ideas.copy: Try the revised process with a few people in their normal working conditions. Observe where they hesitate or need help. Use completion, errors, and their feedback to decide what to improve next.
ideas.question: “Can someone use this successfully without us explaining it?”

takeaway: A practical way to improve a process: observe real work, remove unnecessary effort, and test with the people who use it—so the design holds up beyond the flowchart.

title: We’ve Always Done It This Way Is Data
navLabel: We’ve Always Done It This Way
subtitle: Get curious before you change it.
premise: Long-standing habits can carry hard-won knowledge about customers, risk, and what has gone wrong before. They can also outlive the problem they solved. This talk helps leaders listen to that history, test what still matters, and involve employees in shaping what comes next.

ideas.statement: History is part of the evidence.
ideas.title: Find the reason behind the routine.
ideas.copy: Ask how the practice began and what people learned along the way. A repeated step may protect a customer, prevent a familiar error, or compensate for a limitation that was never fixed.
ideas.question: “What problem was this originally trying to solve?”

ideas.statement: A good reason can stop being relevant.
ideas.title: Check what still holds true.
ideas.copy: Compare the original reason with the conditions today. Look for evidence that the risk, constraint, or customer need still exists. Identify what remains useful and what is being carried forward on assumption.
ideas.question: “What would tell us this is still necessary?”

ideas.statement: People can help shape what comes next.
ideas.title: Build on what people know.
ideas.copy: Invite the people closest to the work to help design a small change. Preserve what still serves a purpose, name the uncertainty, and agree on what you will watch as you try a different approach.
ideas.question: “What could we try while protecting what still matters?”

takeaway: A practical way to lead change: uncover the original purpose, test today’s assumptions, and involve people in a change you can try, learn from, and improve.
